This summer broke temperature records in western Europe and made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists. Photograph: Annice Lyn/Getty Images Opinion Extreme heat Cities sweltering and the smell of the middle ages: has the climate crisis killed Instagram’s Euro summer? Brigid Delaney Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven? Tue 1 Sep 2026 01.03 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 05.15 EDT Share This week the Euro summer comes to an end – and so does a certain type of posting on Instagram. Waiting at the bus stop in the grey winter dawn, a slanting rain soaking your trouser leg, you can warm yourself by scrolling your feed and seeing pictures of Australians enjoying a Euro summer. There it is again – azure Greek coves, plates of barbecued sardines, the yachts rented by the hour, and selfies on the balcony of some Paris Airbnb, drinking wine in the long, blue night. But this year, just out of the frame but never far away, was the heat . You can’t easily photograph heat but it infused the season so monumentally that it might just have killed the Euro summer dream cold. With extreme heat starting in late May, this summer broke temperature records in western Europe and made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists. France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing land Read more Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven? How aspirational and glamorous is it to spend your days in an air-conditioned shopping centre (if you can find one) because to try to see a cathedral or historic site is to risk heatstroke? To travel to the usual European vacation spots in high season now is to endure. It’s to plan your travel so that you aren’t outside in the middle of the day. It’s to stay in places that have air conditioning – if you can find them – and pay a premium to try to stay cool. It’s major monuments and attractions being closed because it’s too dangerous for them to remain open. (In June, Notre-Dame Cathedral restricted access to its towers , while the Eiffel Tower, which is normally open late, announced a 4pm closure, as did the Louvre.) It’s the cities sweltering, smelling of the middle ages – decomposing rubbish, sweat and hot bodies. It’s the feeling of being drained of energy, jet-lagged and damp, lying on a hard mattress in your shuttered hotel room, face close to the fan, as the thick air turns. It’s a population driven mad by the weather, throwing themselves into the canals at 2am because the heat gets trapped in their apartments at night, making it impossible to cool down and sleep. Travel is meant to be pleasurable. Holidays are supposed to be relaxing. But heat of this intensity and duration is incompatible with tourism. It becomes dangerous. Take, for example, the new trees planted to provide shade in Rome’s Piazza Risorgimento, near St Peter’s Basilica. They were burnt to a crisp, according to CNN , and the benches in dark plastic and wood were searingly hot and unable to be used. Across Europe, critical infrastructure failed – with overheated signal systems, melting asphalt that affected tram tracks, and train rails buckling in the extreme heat. As well as making things outside unbearable and dangerous, the weather creates its own confusion and disorientation in the body. When you have heatstroke , you need to sweat to cool down but your skin stays parched and dry. Your body craves fluid but you get confused and forget to drink. At least 35,000 more people died than expected in Europe this summer due to back-to-back heatwaves, with heatstroke a culprit. I t’s a strange aspect of human psychology that once summer passes we can remember it was hot , we can remember it was horrible , but the actual sensations of physical and mental distress we experienced fade. The body forgets, until next time. The brain stores the fact of heat but not the sensation. But now is the time to prepare for next year, which could be even hotter . Australia is imperfect when it comes to climate adaptation and often our approach has been reactionary, piecemeal and ad hoc. But we have experience with long and increasingly uncomfortable summers – and over the years some approaches have been useful. ‘It’s like a furnace’: French struggle with heat-trap homes as climate inequality grows Read more Develop public education campaigns about the sun and its power. Erect shade cloths in schools and public places. Introduce sunhats as part of your childrens’ school uniforms in summer. Rethink work from home rules if workers don’t have access to air conditioning at home, or consider splitting the working day so workers without cooling are not working in the hottest parts of the day. Make major investments in urban design that presume more extreme temperatures (large plazas like those seen all over Europe are not suitable for our changing climate, as stone absorbs and radiates heat ferociously). Install air conditioning or other cooling measures on public transport, in offices and public buildings. Plant more trees. Install water fountains across public spaces, indoor and outdoor. Have labour laws that protect workers who are on building sites or outdoors in extreme conditions, and make those conditions mandatory. Introduce a heat-warning system with legal obligations attached (ie school and outdoor work cancelled, outdoor events cancelled). Make it socially acceptable to wear shorts to the office . And the other big change to consider? Australians could skip the annual Euro summer pilgrimage and enjoy the chill in the air at home. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/17/trum.text: US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive a new package of sanctions and tariffs on Russia shortly before it was due to take effect, telling Congress it was in the US' national interest.Trump had signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" into law in September in a push to increase pressure on the Kremlin and the Russian economy.The legislation - named in honour of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the measures - had sought to impose sanctions on Russian government and military officials, major banks, and vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. It also provided for duties on Russian goods and goods from certain countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has called the decision to put the sanctions on hold a "significant and truly historic moment," adding that the package could have "brought economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a complete standstill."Trump's move comes amid his increasing criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.It also follows a controversial announcement from Trump, who is gearing up for the US' midterm elections, earlier this month on a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to release large flows of diesel into global markets in an effort to bring down fuel prices."It was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."Zelenskyy in BrusselsThe Ukrainian leader has been in Brussels this week, where he has been meeting with European leaders to discuss the ongoing war.Taking questions from the media on Friday, Zelenskyy was asked whether he felt he had been made a "scapegoat" for Trump's "own problems" ahead of November's midterms.He gave a wry smile and said: "This is my answer."Addressing the US-Russia diesel deal, Zelenskyy added that Ukraine "can’t accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next.""I’m absolutely sure of that," he said. "After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don’t defend that through diplomacy – who will do it for us?"

https://www.bursa.ro/the-balance-sheet-o.text: September found Romania in the same state of limbo that marked the end of summer: a dismissed government forced to handle issues beyond the scope of an interim cabinet, political parties unable to form a majority, and an economy where every political delay risked translating into additional costs. The nomination of Siegfried Mureşan offered a prospect for ending the deadlock, but the vote on September 30 ended the month with a new failure. The proposed cabinet secured only 182 votes-51 short of the number required for investiture. By month's end, 148 days had passed since the dismissal of the Bolojan government. Compounding this crisis was a scandal sparked by international media reports concerning the US Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, and the promotion of American liquefied natural gas in the region. Statements attributed to the diplomat regarding the potential ousting of governments, her meetings with Romanian politicians, and disputes over the advisability of gas purchases shifted the debate from the commercial realm to issues of sovereignty and political accountability. However, journalistic confirmation of certain statements did not amount to proof of American intervention in the dismissal of the Bucharest government. On the streets, the sheep farmers' protest demonstrated how quickly economic grievances can merge with political radicalization. Within state institutions, the reform of state-owned companies brought to light a portfolio of nearly 1,900 enterprises, over a thousand of which met the criteria for restructuring analysis. Meanwhile, at the Ministry of Finance, efforts to correct the deficit continued alongside pressures stemming from interest payments, subsidies, and outstanding obligations to energy suppliers. The budgetary picture remained the authorities' primary selling point: the eight-month deficit dropped to 2.89% of GDP, and investment spending rose. However, the state had already paid 42.05 billion lei in interest, the National Bank of Romania's foreign exchange reserves had shrunk by 4.805 billion euros in a single month, and the impending deadline for the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) forced institutions to work under the pressure of the final payment request. Romania ended September with a visible fiscal adjustment but an unresolved political issue. *Siegfried Mureşan: Prime Minister-designate without a secure majority Following the withdrawal of Eugen Tomac and the rejection of the Adrian Veştea Cabinet, President Nicuşor Dan turned to Siegfried Mureşan to form a new government. The candidate's European experience and negotiating skills were the key arguments for his nomination; however, consultations at Cotroceni Palace had failed to yield an agreement among the parties. The PSD claimed the premiership, the PNL and USR supported Mureşan, while AUR made its support conditional on its own participation in the government. The UDMR warned that the prime minister's profile could not substitute for a parliamentary majority. Options involving a technocratic prime minister or successive minority governments were also discussed, yet none of these variants resulted in an agreement. The nomination thus shifted the political test to Parliament. Nicuşor Dan criticized the parties' electoral preoccupations and emphasized the need for a government capable of passing the budget revision. Siegfried Mureşan agreed to attempt forming the Cabinet but faced the same obstacle that had blocked previous attempts: the support pledged by certain parties was insufficient for investiture. Hearings held on September 28 and 29 revealed the limited willingness to compromise. On September 30, the Mureşan Cabinet was rejected by the plenary session of Parliament. The 182 votes in favor confirmed that negotiations had failed to overcome opposition from the PSD and AUR. Romania remained dependent on an executive with limited powers precisely during the period when the budget for the following year was being prepared. The debate pitted two interpretations of economic adjustment against each other. Supporters of the Cabinet presented the reduction of waste and state reform as prerequisites for recovery, whereas the PSD characterized the continuation of Bolojan's policies as a perpetuation of austerity, and AUR called for early elections. Kelemen Hunor, the UDMR leader, warned that society was losing both patience and confidence. The failure to confirm the government did not suspend the state's economic obligations. Payments, projects, and the preparation of budgetary decisions had to continue, while any measure exceeding the interim administration's mandate depended on fresh parliamentary negotiations. *The Guilfoyle Scandal: US gas at the heart of the political crisis On September 26, the Wall Street Journal published an article about a discussion held in Athens in March between Kimberly Guilfoyle and the Greek Minister of Energy. According to the report, the ambassador allegedly referred to the imminent fall of the Romanian government and the US's capacity to bring about such changes in other countries. The diplomat's lawyer disputed the description of the conversation. The "Financial Times" later independently confirmed the statement attributed to the ambassador and placed the conversation at a dinner on March 18. However, the publication noted that it was unclear whether Guilfoyle had advised the Social Democrats to leave the government. This distinction remains crucial: reporting a claim about political influence and demonstrating the actual exercise of that influence are two different things. Images from the March 31 meeting at the Isoletta restaurant-attended by Sorin Grindeanu, Bogdan Ivan, presidential advisor Florin Vlădică, and Guilfoyle-fueled the controversy. Grindeanu maintained that the discussions focused on the Vertical Corridor and rejected the allegations, while George Simion denied the existence of any such agreements. The government stated that no discussions had taken place between the Prime Minister's Chancellery and the ambassador, and that no document committing Romania to liquefied natural gas (LNG) purchases had been approved. The executive distinguished between the development of transit infrastructure and the actual purchase of gas. Beyond the diplomatic statements, the controversy highlighted the economic terms of a potential purchase. According to documents presented by the domestic media, Romgaz had rejected a proposal to purchase American LNG in December 2025, estimating that the terms could have resulted in annual losses of euro50-300 million. Media reports indicate that Energy Minister Bogdan Ivan attempted to persuade the company again in February-albeit unsuccessfully-and that the Ministry of Energy's Control Body initiated an inspection at Romgaz that same month. The company confirmed the start of the inspection on February 16, noting that its objective was to review the investment at Iernut. In a statement issued on September 28, Romgaz explicitly denied that any Romanian official had exerted pressure to conclude a gas purchase or sale contract. The company cited corporate governance rules and the practice of basing decisions on economic, commercial, and strategic criteria. *Deficit drops by nearly RON 27 billion; interest payments reach RON 42 billion The eight-month budget execution report, presented by the Ministry of Finance on September 26, confirmed the ongoing fiscal adjustment. The consolidated general government deficit stood at RON 59.42 billion, down from RON 86.36 billion during the same period in 2025. This represented a nominal reduction of RON 26.94 billion (approximately 31%), with the deficit-to-GDP ratio falling from 4.51% to 2.89%. Total revenues rose by 11.4% to 468.10 billion lei, while expenditures increased by 4.2% to 527.53 billion lei. VAT receipts reached 103.35 billion lei, 25.2% above the level recorded in the first eight months of 2025. Tax revenues totaled 242.69 billion lei, and funds received from the European Union and other donors rose by 37.7% to 43.38 billion lei. Personnel expenses decreased by 4.26 billion lei, falling to 109.04 billion lei. Investments climbed from 71.95 billion lei to 97.05 billion lei, an increase of 25.1 billion lei. European funding and the NRRP (National Recovery and Resilience Plan) supported this trend, offsetting the reduction in investments from national sources. However, debt pressure continued to rise. Interest payments totaled 42.05 billion lei-an increase of 8.86 billion lei, or 26.7%, over the 2025 level. This amount was nearly equal to the total revenue from wage and income taxes, which stood at 42.86 billion lei. While deficit correction improved the current situation, an increasingly large share of state resources remained consumed by debt servicing. *NRRP: Awaiting the final payment request The report presented to the Government on September 3 outlined the status of the NRRP following the deadline for completing investments and reforms. The first four payment requests had been submitted and assessed; however, regarding the third request, euro869.81 million remained suspended due to six milestones not having been satisfactorily met. The fifth request, submitted on August 14, covered 75 targets and milestones and had a net value of euro2.085 billion. For the final request, authorities indicated a deadline of September 30 and a net value of euro4.348 billion, comprising euro2.582 billion in grants and euro1.765 billion in loans. Together, the two requests amounted to approximately euro6.43 billion. Their value did not equate to funds already received, and the announced timeline for the final request did not, in itself, confirm its submission or approval. Payment was contingent upon the European Commission's assessment and the fulfillment of the agreed-upon conditions. Against this backdrop, the extension of the interim mandate maintained the separation between project administration and executive authority to adopt the necessary legislative reforms. The state had to close a key investment program at a time when it remained impossible to build a political majority to steer it. On September 30, the Government officially submitted the final payment request under the NRRP to the European Commission, amounting to euro6.04 billion before the deduction of pre-financing. According to the Ministry of Investments and European Projects, the net amount requested by the country is euro4,347,770,169: euro2,582,415,100 in non-repayable European funds and euro1,765,355,069 in the form of a loan. *Foreign exchange reserves drop by euro4.8 billion in one month As of September 30, the National Bank of Romania's (BNR) foreign exchange reserves stood at euro60.06 billion, down from euro64.865 billion at the end of August. The reduction amounted to euro4.805 billion, or approximately 7.4%, in a single month. The BNR reported inflows of euro3.302 billion and outflows of euro8.107 billion. These operations included changes in banks' minimum foreign currency reserves, movements in the Ministry of Finance's accounts, and payments from the European Commission's account. Principal and interest payments on foreign-currency public debt accounted for approximately euro2.684 billion of the outflows. Data published by the NBR does not allow the entire decline to be attributed to a single cause. Gold reserves remained at 103.6 tonnes, valued at euro12.280 billion. Total international reserves-comprising foreign currency and gold-fell from euro77.627 billion to euro72.340 billion. For October, foreign-currency public debt payments due were estimated at approximately euro350 million. Also in September, the NBR published its annual survey on foreign direct investment for 2025, showing a net inflow of euro7.907 billion and a stock of euro134.823 billion at the end of that year. Earnings realized by non-resident investors amounted to euro11.493 billion. These figures describe the previous year and the economy's investment base, without indicating a rebound in flows in September 2026. *Over one thousand state-owned companies subject to restructuring analysis On September 18, the Government received the preliminary results of an inventory of public enterprises. Out of a total of 1,868 companies, 1,098 met the technical criteria for an analysis regarding restructuring and portfolio reduction. A total of 533 enterprises-representing 28.5% of the total-had failed to submit their financial statements for the previous year on time. Meeting these criteria did not imply the automatic closure of the companies. The supervising authorities were required to provide a rationale for either maintaining or restructuring each company, accompanied by specific measures and an implementation timeline. The statutory deadline for mandating portfolio reduction measures was June 30, 2027, with the results of the requested analyses due within 20 working days and subject to monthly monitoring. The launch of the "guvernanta.gov.ro" platform introduced a transparency component, providing information on 121 active central government-owned companies and over 1,350 documents regarding their management teams. Aggregated data revealed more than 100 individuals holding at least two simultaneous positions, 115 individuals with monthly incomes between 25,000 and 50,000 lei, 36 earning between 50,000 and 100,000 lei, and one individual earning over 100,000 lei. Publishing details on mandates and remuneration made the cost of management teams more visible. However, the true test of the reform remained the state's ability to link these costs to performance outcomes and to justify the retention of each equity stake. *Sheep farmers protest; interim government limits authorities' response The protest on September 15 brought sheep farmers' grievances regarding exports, sanitary measures, compensation, and feed costs to Victory Square. The demonstration escalated into violence, and gendarmes removed 30 individuals for identification and questioning. The media documented the presence of participants known for supporting Călin Georgescu and for their involvement in other demonstrations. The government maintained that six meetings with sector representatives had taken place since July and that the ANSVSA had submitted a plan to the European Commission to unblock exports. A draft law existed to compensate for additional feed costs, but its adoption fell to Parliament, given the absence of a fully empowered executive. The following day, the farmers' delegation left the Cotroceni Palace dissatisfied after talks with a presidential advisor. Representatives of the protesters even raised the possibility of traveling to Brussels. The promise to resume dialogue once a new government was installed highlighted the core issue: farmers needed immediate solutions, whereas institutions made part of the response contingent on resolving the political crisis. Regarding support for farmers, on September 18, the executive approved 155.36 million lei for growers of corn and sunflower crops affected by the 2025 drought, with funding split equally between European funds and the national budget. The maximum support was 333 lei per hectare for fully affected areas, with reductions applied based on the extent of the damage. Separately, the agricultural diesel scheme received an additional 149.37 million lei. These measures provided resources to the agricultural sector, though they did not address all the demands of the sheep farming industry. *State releases energy payments; diesel prices remain under pressure In September, the Ministry of Finance increased the Ministry of Labour's spending limit by 1.058 billion lei. Approximately 1.03 billion lei was earmarked for reimbursements to cover electricity and natural gas consumption costs. Minister Alexandru Nazare

https://www.dw.com/en/norway-s-ice-hocke.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PG7Q Prefer DW on Google The last time Germany hosted the World Championship in 2017, Russia won the bronze medal Image: Andreas Dick/Beautiful Sports/IMAGO Advertisement With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part. The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF , comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey." As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule. Carney: 'Russians will not be there' However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility. "While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney. "So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there." How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland , Sweden , Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete. "This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten. "The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days." Hosts Germany continue to explore options Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May. "We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday. While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome. Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort. On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place." Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place. "At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese. However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility. Could Munich's Olympic bid be a factor? It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044 . The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine. The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead. Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications." Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.
